directive: The new Roman-authorized expedition continues from its first camp while established estate administration, correspondence, and agricultural threads continue independently.

events.title: THE EXPEDITION LEAVES ITS FIRST CAMP AND ENTERS ROUGHER COUNTRY
events.body: The expedition leaves its first camp and moves beyond the ground examined on the previous day. The route becomes narrower and the party proceeds more cautiously, with the day's march shaped by the condition of the ground rather than by a fixed distance. Observations from the first camp are carried forward with the expedition records. The movement marks the first sustained advance into country that remains unfamiliar to Valerius and his companions.

events.title: A LOCAL GUIDE DISAGREES WITH AN EARLIER ROUTE ACCOUNT
events.body: A local guide gives the expedition a route account that differs from one received before departure. The disagreement concerns the condition of a crossing farther ahead rather than the existence of the route itself. The expedition scribes record both accounts separately. Valerius's party continues gathering information before committing itself to the crossing.

events.title: SPRING WORKERS REPORT A STRONGER DEMAND FOR WATER ON THE NEW TRACT
events.body: Word reaches the estate that the newly incorporated fields are drawing heavier water demand as spring work intensifies. The stewards compare the request with the watering arrangement already established for nearby smallholders. The additional work is accommodated without reopening the ownership question settled by the purchase. The increased demand consumes part of the estate's available supply resources, and the report gives the estate a clearer picture of the practical demands created by the expanded acreage.

events.title: METELLUS CELER'S CORRESPONDENCE IS ADDED TO THE EXPEDITION PAPERS
events.body: A message associated with Quintus Caecilius Metellus Celer is preserved alongside the expedition correspondence. It concerns the usefulness of careful observations and the preservation of documentary material rather than directing Valerius's route. The scribes mark the message as a separate Roman political correspondence item. Its presence reinforces the continuing connection between Valerius's field activity and the Roman circles already following his affairs.

events.title: THE ESTATE'S SPRING ACCOUNTS ARE KEPT SEPARATE FROM THE EXPEDITION RECORDS
events.body: The estate administration closes another set of spring entries while the expedition remains away from the household's ordinary routine. Estate and expedition records are kept separate so that field observations cannot be confused with household accounts. The separation allows the expedition papers to accumulate independently while the estate continues its established administration. No new harvest, sale, rent receipt, payment, or investment return is realized in these entries.

events.title: THE EXPEDITION REACHES ITS FIRST DIFFICULT PASS
events.body: You begin the morning with the road already climbing ahead of you, the easier ground of the previous marches giving way to broken slopes and loose stone. The expedition's purpose is to continue the newly authorized Roman journey into unfamiliar country and produce a firsthand geographic record; no named final destination is established in the surviving campaign record. The campaign's military ledger records 394 soldiers overall, but it does not establish a separate numerical strength for this expedition detachment, so no invented detachment size is assigned. The route narrows until the column can no longer maintain the comfortable pace of the earlier days. You order the heavier loads redistributed so that the animals are not forced upward under unnecessary strain. You leave the head of the column and walk part of the ascent yourself, testing the ground before asking the rest of the expedition to follow. The surface shifts beneath your sandals as the slope steepens. There is no enemy waiting above you and no sudden disaster; the difficulty comes from the country itself. You stop repeatedly to examine the slope, the footing, and the line by which the animals can pass safely. Ahead, the apparent end of the route seems to leave the expedition facing a dead slope, but closer inspection reveals that the path bends toward a lower saddle. The discovery changes the day's movement. The pass is usable, but it will take longer than the route reports had suggested. You order the pace reduced rather than forcing the column forward merely to satisfy an expected distance. The men adjust their movement and the expedition climbs steadily, sacrificing speed for control. By midday you reach the saddle. From there the country opens unexpectedly, revealing several possible routes beyond the pass. You compare what you can see with the conflicting reports recorded two days earlier. One account now appears more plausible than the other, but you do not erase the weaker report simply because the landscape has given you a better impression of the route. You descend far enough to inspect the beginning of the next stage yourself. The ground beyond the saddle remains unfamiliar, and the expedition has not reached any final destination. With daylight becoming less useful for a safe continuation, you select a position for the night's camp rather than attempting to force another difficult stage. That evening, the scribes assemble the day's observations while the expedition settles around the camp. You review the route, the terrain, the water situation, and the conflicting testimony preserved from earlier travelers. The pass becomes the first substantial geographic obstacle personally crossed during this new expedition. There is no treasure, captured settlement, spectacular city, or convenient revelation waiting beyond it. What you have gained is more practical: a tested route, a firsthand description of the terrain, and a clearer understanding of how unreliable local route reports can be when conditions change. You make certain the record distinguishes what you personally observed from what travelers told the expedition. Measurements and direct observations are preserved separately from testimony. The distinction matters because the expedition's purpose is not merely to collect stories but to produce a record that can withstand later scrutiny. The country beyond the camp remains unknown. You have not completed the expedition, reached a final destination, or returned to Rome. You have only crossed its first major geographic obstacle and established the next point from which the journey can continue. The men settle for the night with the road behind them and unfamiliar country ahead. The pass has not ended the expedition; it has given it its first tested route. Tomorrow's movement will begin from this new camp, carrying forward the observations made today.

events.title: THE FIRST PASS ACCOUNT IS COPIED INTO THE EXPEDITION'S PERMANENT RECORD
events.body: The expedition scribes copy the account of the difficult pass into the permanent field record. Measurements and route observations are kept together with the local statements that preceded the crossing, allowing the written account to distinguish direct observation from testimony. The day's copy is sealed before the party prepares for the next movement. The expedition therefore ends the week with its first substantial route feature documented from direct experience.
